neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 9 (E2V3M4). Minimally responsive. Does not follow commands. Eye opening to pain. Incomprehensible sounds. Purposeful withdrawal to pain. Asterixis cannot be assessed — GCS too low. Girlfriend reports he had a convulsive event 30 minutes before ambulance called.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4 mm, equal, sluggishly reactive. Doll's eye reflex intact. No nystagmus.
neurological_exam.motor: Minimal spontaneous movement. Purposeful withdrawal pain.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses extensor (Babinski) bilaterally.
neurological_exam.additional: GCS 9 — severely depressed consciousness after witnessed convulsive episode. Tongue laceration noted. Urinary incontinence during episode. Bilateral extensor plantar responses suggest post-ictal state or severe cerebral dysfunction. This could be: (1) prolonged postictal state from new seizure in known seizure disorder, (2) non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) after seizure, (3) severe HE (grade IV) presenting with GCS 9, or (4) any combination.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F. is a 44-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis, prior seizure disorder treated with levetiracetam, and an established HE prophylaxis regimen, who was brought by ambulance in an unresponsive state. His girlfriend witnessed him having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure approximately 30 minutes before EMS arrival. He had been increasingly confused over the prior 2-3 days — she attributed it to usual HE episodes which he has had twice before. On the morning of presentation, he was more confused than usual, and then she found him on the floor seizing. He had been compliant with rifaximin and lactulose. He is 1 year sober. His levetiracetam had been recently increased from 500 mg BID to 1000 mg BID by his neurologist 3 weeks ago — girlfriend reports he may have missed some doses in the past week ('he kept forgetting'). On arrival he remains unresponsive with a GCS of 9.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Non-convulsive status epilepticus following breakthrough generalized tonic-clonic seizure (subtherapeutic levetiracetam 8 µg/mL) with concurrent severe hepatic encephalopathy (ammonia 108) in alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 12); both lower consciousness to GCS 9.

differential.diagnosis: Severe hepatic encephalopathy (sole cause of GCS 9)
differential.key_features: Ammonia 108 + cirrhosis + asterixis = HE; but EEG is essential — cannot distinguish severe HE from NCSE clinically.
Post-ictal usually resolves within 30-60 minutes; persistence beyond raises NCSE concern.

differential.diagnosis: Anoxic brain injury from prolonged seizure
differential.key_features: MRI DWI if prolonged hypoxia; airway assessment.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, CMP, ammonia, magnesium, lactate, coagulation, CK. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia 108; levetiracetam level (subtherapeutic 8 µg/mL); cirrhosis features; CK if prolonged seizure; cultures.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.
Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (NCSE diagnosis; Salzburg EEG criteria; levetiracetam dosing in cirrhosis).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering levetiracetam (LOAD and adjust dose), lactulose, rifaximin, second AED if NCSE confirmed (avoid valproate in cirrhosis); flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.action: Continuous EEG (cEEG) — required to exclude NCSE in any patient with persistent unresponsiveness after seizure; the single most important test in this case.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Rhythmic or periodic discharges meeting NCSE criteria, vs generalized slowing alone; benzodiazepine challenge clarifies if pattern is responsive.

optimal_actions.action: Consult neurology + hepatology + critical care — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Pyuria and bacteriuria identify a urinary source; a negative result removes it from the list of precipitants

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Continuous EEG to exclude NCSE — this is the critical test for this case.
Levetiracetam IV load (60 mg/kg up to 4.5 g) and resume daily dosing; consider lacosamide as adjunct (no hepatic dose adjustment needed; safer than valproate in cirrhosis).
Lactulose 30-45 mL TID and rifaximin 550 mg BID for HE.
Empiric thiamine 500 mg IV before dextrose.
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not use valproate as second-line AED in cirrhosis — hyperammonemia + hepatic toxicity risks.
Avoid scheduled benzodiazepines as AED for HE-prone patients; use them ONLY for acute seizure termination (lorazepam 2 mg IV), then transition to levetiracetam/lacosamide.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Persistent unresponsiveness after a witnessed seizure mandates continuous EEG to exclude NCSE — clinical examination cannot distinguish severe HE from NCSE.
Cirrhotic patients on AEDs need adherence and level monitoring — subtherapeutic levels are a common breakthrough trigger.
Lacosamide and levetiracetam are AEDs of choice in cirrhosis (no significant hepatic adjustment).
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: EEG shows non-specific slowing and triphasic waves; the diagnosis is clinical with ammonia and precipitant identification.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Post-ictal states typically resolve within 30-60 minutes; persistent unresponsiveness requires cEEG to exclude NCSE.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Severe HE and NCSE are clinically indistinguishable; both can coexist. cEEG is mandatory.
